coreTruths.title: Plaque biofilm is the primary cause of virtually all periodontal disease
coreTruths.broaderContext: Periodontitis is one of the two main reasons people lose teeth. Plaque drives it, which makes plaque control the highest-leverage daily habit in dentistry.
coreTruths.body:
## The microbial community shifts as inflammation deepens

Almost every form of periodontal disease starts with plaque [1]. Healthy gums carry mostly Gram-positive aerobes and facultative anaerobes. As plaque builds up and inflammation sets in, the population shifts toward anaerobes and Gram-negative species. Established periodontitis runs on anaerobic Gram-negative rods [2].

## Treatment starts with disrupting the biofilm, not antibiotics

Every plan starts with breaking up the plaque. Disrupt the biofilm and the disease backs off [3]. OHI, scaling, and root surface debridement are not extras, they are the treatment. Antibiotics are not a shortcut [4]. Surgery only comes after non-surgical control has been tried [5], because cutting tissue without sorting out plaque just rebuilds the same problem.

## Gingivitis is the early stage of bone loss

Gingivitis comes first. There is no evidence periodontitis develops without it [6]. So treating gingivitis is bone-loss prevention, not just tidying up bleeding gums. Left alone, those bleeding gums are the start of a process that can reach bone in susceptible patients.

citations.quote: The 1° aetiology of virtually all forms of periodontal disease is plaque. It exists in a biofilm at the supragingival margin and can progress subgingivally.

Clinically healthy gingivae are associated with a high proportion of Gram +ve rods and cocci which are facultatively anaerobic or aerobic. Gingivitis is associated with an ↑ number of facultative anaerobes, strict anaerobes, and an ↑ number of Gram –ve rods. Established periodontitis is associated with a majority presence of anaerobic Gram –ve rods.

Periodontal disease is an infection due to the presence of plaque biofilm, therefore, disruption of the plaque biofilm and control of plaque is the key to success. More complex Rx will always fail in the absence of effective plaque control.

There are few reasons to use antimicrobials in periodontal therapy. The plaque biofilm affects the response, concentration in gingival crevicular fluid is low, antibiotics have side effects, and there is the growing problem of antibiotic resistance. Antibiotics are not really justified for use in chronic periodontitis.
Periodontal surgery is mostly considered after a course of non-surgical debridement.

The direct association between the presence of tooth surface plaque and gingivitis has been confirmed. Gingivitis precedes periodontitis but there is no evidence to suggest that periodontitis develops in the absence of gingivitis.

coreTruths.title: Periodontal tissue destruction is host-mediated, not direct bacterial damage
coreTruths.broaderContext: Plaque triggers periodontitis but the host's immune response does the damage. That is why smoking and diabetes shape outcomes, and why they belong in the periodontal plan.
coreTruths.body:
## The host's immune response does most of the damage

Plaque triggers periodontitis. The host's own immune response does most of the actual damage [1]. Bacteria deliver virulence factors and inflammatory mediators, but the bone loss and attachment loss come from the prolonged inflammatory and immune reaction, not the bugs directly.

## Susceptibility sits with the host: smoking and diabetes are the big modifiers

Two patients with the same plaque can have very different bone loss. The difference sits with the host. The two big modifiers in real practice are smoking and poorly controlled diabetes [2], which both turn up the inflammatory volume. That is why the current diagnosis statement names risk factors alongside stage and grade, with smoking the textbook example [3].

## Therapy that ignores the host is half a treatment

Periodontal therapy that skips host risk factors is half a treatment. A smoking cessation conversation, and where it applies a quick liaison with the GP about diabetic control, belong in the periodontal plan [4], not in someone else's clinic. Cleaning a smoker's mouth without mentioning the smoking is leaving the bigger lever untouched.

citations.quote: The host response to the biofilm is meant to be protective but can also cause local tissue damage. Both inflammatory and immunologically mediated pathways can contribute to periodontal damage.

Although mild to moderate periodontitis is common, severe periodontitis affects a relatively small subset of the population. Certain risk factors such as smoking, poorly controlled diabetes, and colonization by specific bacteria at high levels have been identified.
Generalized periodontitis stage III grade B currently unstable with smoking as a risk factor.
This is where the aim is to control plaque and address modifiable risk factors (e.g. smoking cessation counselling, liaise with GMP if poorly controlled diabetes).

coreTruths.title: Oral health is a balanced ecosystem; disease is dysbiosis, not infection by an invader
coreTruths.broaderContext: Modern dentistry treats the mouth as an ecosystem to balance, not an infection to clear. This shapes how cleaning works, why maintenance matters, and why antibiotics rarely fix it.
coreTruths.body:
## The healthy mouth is balanced, not sterile

The healthy mouth is not a sterile place. It carries a balanced community of more than 700 bacterial species, mostly working with the host rather than against it. The resident flora actually keeps outside microbes from getting a foothold [1].

## Disease is a shift in the balance, not a single invader

Periodontitis is not one invading organism. It is a shift in the community balance. The current model is called symbiosis-dysbiosis: when the biofilm is not disrupted often enough, organisms like Fusobacterium nucleatum tilt the local ecology toward pathogens such as P. gingivalis. In susceptible patients the host response that follows is what does the tissue damage [2].

## The aim of cleaning is rebalance, not sterilisation

The aim is to keep the ecology in symbiosis. Disrupting the biofilm at recall, plus good daily home care, is enough for most patients [3]. Antibiotics get used only when the ecology has tipped past what cleaning can fix on its own [4].

## Maintenance holds a balance, it does not cure an infection

Recall in a treated patient is about holding the balance, not chasing a new infection [5]. Visits start at 3–4 monthly intervals and can stretch to 6 months once things stay stable [6]. Stop maintenance and the ecology drifts back toward dysbiosis.

citations.quote: More than 700 different species can colonize the mouth and >400 species may be found in periodontal pockets. Resident oral microflora form multi-species biofilms on oral surfaces. In health there is a balanced relationship between oral microflora and the host which is mutually beneficial. The resident microflora are important in preventing colonization by exogenous microbes.

if the biofilm is not disrupted regularly, certain species such as Fusobacterium nucleatum are favoured. These enable a stronger host response and thus create the conditions that promote the development and growth of traditional pathogens such as P. gingivalis. This is known as incipient dysbiosis because in non-susceptible individuals the inflammation does not progress beyond gingivitis. However, in susceptible individuals incipient dysbiosis can trigger a host response that is excessive, resulting in collateral periodontal tissue damage.

Periodontal disease is an infection due to the presence of plaque biofilm, therefore, disruption of the plaque biofilm and control of plaque is the key to success. More complex Rx will always fail in the absence of effective plaque control.

There are few reasons to use antimicrobials in periodontal therapy. The plaque biofilm affects the response, concentration in gingival crevicular fluid is low, antibiotics have side effects, and there is the growing problem of antibiotic resistance. Antibiotics are not really justified for use in chronic periodontitis.
To avoid further attachment loss and to maintain the therapeutic benefits, long-term patients require monitoring and sometimes Rx to support their own home care.
Then maintenance visits begin at 3–4-monthly intervals and may be lengthened up to 6 months if appropriate although there is no good evidence for the ideal frequency of maintenance visits.

coreTruths.title: The BPE is a screening tool that points to the next step, not a diagnosis
coreTruths.broaderContext: The BPE shapes most periodontal decisions in general practice. Treating it as a diagnosis rather than a screen leads to under-investigation in the very patients who need more.
coreTruths.body:
## The BPE tells the clinician where to look harder, not what is wrong

The BPE is a simple screening tool that decides what further examination is needed and points to the next phase of treatment [1]. It records the highest score per sextant, so it deliberately hides site-by-site detail. A code is a flag, not a diagnosis.

## Codes 3 and above need a six-point chart, not just a clean

For codes 0, 1, or 2, the BPE keeps getting repeated at follow-up. For codes 3 and 4, a more detailed periodontal charting and further treatment is required [2]. A code 4 means at least one pocket greater than 6mm somewhere in that sextant; without a full chart the clinician cannot say which tooth, how deep, or how unstable.

## The BPE cannot be used to monitor treatment

Because the BPE only records the worst score per sextant, it cannot show how individual sites change after treatment. The BPE cannot be used to monitor the response to periodontal Rx [3]. Six-point pocket charts, bleeding scores, and standardised radiographs do that job.

## BPE is not for implants

BPE probing is not appropriate at implant sites [4]. The soft tissue cuff around an implant is not the same as around a tooth, so peri-implant tissues are less resistant to probing. Six-point pocket charting is recommended around implants instead [4].

citations.quote: The BPE is a simple screening tool that will be used to determine what further examination is needed and therefore provides a direction of the next phase of Rx.
For patients with BPE codes 3 and 4, further detailed periodontal charting would be needed and further Rx as indicated in the following sections.
The BPE cannot be used to monitor the response to periodontal Rx because it cannot provide information on how sites change within a sextant, after Rx. The BPE is a screening tool.
BPE probing is not appropriate for implants sites. The soft tissue connection to implants is not the same as teeth, therefore peri-implant soft tissues are less resistant to probing.

coreTruths.title: A periodontitis diagnosis must carry stage, grade, activity, and risk factors
coreTruths.broaderContext: The 2017 classification turned periodontitis into a four-part profile. It separates how bad it is now from how fast it got there, which is what changes the plan.
coreTruths.body:
## Stage is severity to date; grade is the rate at which it got there

Stage describes the degree of attachment loss and grade describes the rate of progression of the disease to date [1]. In the BSP UK implementation, stage I to IV is set by bone loss as a fraction of root length [2], and grade A to C is set by percentage bone loss divided by patient age [3]. Stage and grade are both assessed on the worst affected tooth [2,3].

## A young patient with moderate bone loss is not the same problem as an older patient with the same bone loss

Grade is what flags rapid progression. The same 30 percent bone loss in a 25-year-old and a 65-year-old is the same stage but a very different grade [3]. Grade C in a young patient changes the urgency, the recall interval, and the threshold for specialist referral.

## Activity decides the next move; pockets that bleed are the unstable ones

A mouth is currently stable, in remission, or unstable. Unstable means probing depth 5mm or more, or 4mm with bleeding [4]. A 5mm or 6mm pocket that does not bleed may not be unstable [5]. So bleeding on probing, not depth alone, drives whether the case still needs active treatment.

## A complete diagnosis names distribution, stage, grade, status, and risk factors

A contemporary diagnosis reads like generalized periodontitis stage III grade B currently unstable with smoking as a risk factor [6]. Listing the risk factor is part of the diagnosis, not an aside, because it is what the next appointment has to act on.

citations.quote: As previously discussed, the staging of the disease describes the degree of attachment loss.

Stage I (early/mild): <15% bone loss or up to 2mm bone loss. Stage II (moderate): bone level in coronal third of root. Stage III (severe): bone level in mid third of root. Stage IV (very severe): bone level in apical third of root. Stage is assessed on the worst affected tooth.
Grading—% bone loss/patient’s age. Grade A (slow): <0.5. Grade B (moderate): 0.5–1.0. Grade C (rapid): >1.0. Grade is assessed on the worst affected tooth.
Currently stable: BOP <10%, PPD <4mm, no BOP at 4mm sites. Currently in remission: BOP >10%, PPD <4mm, no BOP at 4mm sites. Currently unstable: PPD >5mm or PPD >4mm and BOP.
It should be noted that in the BSP implementation document they make the point that a 5mm or 6mm pocket that does not bleed may not be unstable.
As such, an example of a contemporary diagnosis would be ‘generalized periodontitis stage III grade B that is currently unstable with smoking as a risk factor’.

coreTruths.title: Probing pocket depth measures the probe, not the pocket; attachment loss is the truer measure
coreTruths.broaderContext: Pocket depths shift with the gingival margin and with inflammation. Without a fixed reference point, deep pockets can mean disease, swelling, or just a probe pushed too hard.
coreTruths.body:
## A pocket depth without a reference point can mean three different things

Probing pocket depth is measured from the gingival margin to the estimated base of the pocket [1]. The margin moves: inflammation swells it coronally, recession drops it apically, restorations sit wherever they were placed. So the same number can mean different things in different mouths.

## Inflammation makes the probe overshoot, healing makes it undershoot

In inflamed tissue the probe tip pushes through to about 0.5mm apical to the apical extent of the junctional epithelium, which is an overestimate of the real defect [2]. After successful treatment a tight long junctional epithelium can give an underestimate. The probe is not measuring a fixed wound, it is reacting to tissue tone.

## Clinical attachment level uses a fixed landmark

Clinical attachment level is measured from a fixed reference point, the cementoenamel junction or the margin of a restoration, to the base of the pocket [3]. Where recession is present, CAL equals recession plus probing depth [3]. CAL describes the actual loss of support, which is what matters for prognosis and staging.

## Bleeding outranks depth as a marker of activity

Bleeding on probing has been the most useful indicator of disease activity, but only about 30 percent of bleeding sites go on to lose attachment. Absence of bleeding on probing is a strong indicator of periodontal stability [4]. So a deep but non-bleeding pocket can be stable and a shallow but bleeding pocket can be the active one.

citations.quote: Measured from the gingival margin to the estimated base of the pocket.

In the presence of inflammation, a probe tip can pass through the inflamed tissues until it reaches the most coronal dento-gingival fibres, about 0.5mm apical to the apical extent of the junctional epithelium, i.e. an overestimation of the problem. The amount of penetration into the tissues varies directly with the degree of inflammation, so that, following resolution of inflammation, an underestimate of attachment levels may be given.

Measured from a fixed reference point: the cementoenamel junction (CEJ) or margin of a restoration to the base of the pocket. Pockets are therefore dependent on the position of the gingival margin. If recession is present CAL = recession + periodontal probing depth.

Bleeding on probing has traditionally been the most useful indicator of disease activity; however, only 30% of sites which bleed will go on to lose attachment.12 Absence of bleeding on probing is an indicator of periodontal stability.

coreTruths.title: Furcation involvement changes both prognosis and what treatment is realistic
coreTruths.broaderContext: Once the disease reaches the furcation, the geometry of the tooth changes the conversation. Cleaning becomes harder, regeneration becomes less predictable, and extraction enters the discussion.
coreTruths.body:
## Furcation involvement is graded by how far the probe goes

A class 1 furcation lets the probe in less than 3mm; a class 2 goes more than 3mm but does not pass through; a class 3 is a through-and-through defect [1,2,3]. Diagnosis is by probing into the furcation plus radiographs [4]. A radiograph alone underestimates these defects.

## Sensibility-test furcation teeth, the pulp may be involved

The possibility of pulpal pathology is increased in teeth with furcation involvement, so sensibility testing is essential [4]. A periodontal furcation lesion and a pulpal lesion can look similar and travel together.

## Regeneration becomes less predictable as the furcation worsens

Grade 1 furcation defects regenerate more predictably than grade 2; regeneration in grade 3 furcation defects is very poor [5]. So a class 1 might respond to scaling and root debridement, a class 2 may justify GTR with grafts or EMD, and a class 3 often pushes the conversation toward tunnel preparation, root resection, or extraction [3].

## Whatever is done, the patient has to be able to clean it

The surgical technique chosen matters less than the plaque control the patient can keep up afterwards [6]. Mini interproximal brushes are valuable in cleaning furcation defects [6]. If the post-treatment morphology cannot be kept clean by the patient, the procedure will not succeed.

citations.quote: Probe can be inserted <3mm between the roots. Requires scaling and root planing, possibly with furcation plasty.
Horizontal probing depth exceeding 3mm but not extending fully through the width of the furcation area. GTR together with graft materials and EMD can be used to treat class 2 furcations.
Horizontal through-and-through destruction in the furcation area. May require tunnel preparation, &/or root resection, &/or extraction. GTR less predictable with Class 3 defects.
This is established by probing into the furcation and by radiographs. The possibility of pulpal pathology is ↑ in teeth with furcation involvement and sensibility testing is essential.

Three-walled defects have a better chance of regeneration compared to two-walled defects which in turn have a better chance of regeneration than one-walled defects. Horizontal defects are very unpredictable and the chances of regeneration are very poor. Similarly, grade 1 furcation defects have greater predictability compared to grade 2 furcation defects. Regeneration in grade 3 furcation defects is very poor.

It is important to note that the techniques described here are of less significance to long-term outcome than the degree of plaque control that can be achieved and maintained by the patient. Mini interproximal brushes are a valuable aid in cleaning furcation defects and are available in a variety of sizes and shapes.

coreTruths.title: Width of attached gingiva is not decisive for periodontal health
coreTruths.broaderContext: An old rule said the gum needed a few millimetres of attached tissue to survive. Properly designed studies overturned that. Mucogingival surgery is now indication-led, not threshold-led.
coreTruths.body:
## The 3mm rule did not survive proper testing

It was once felt a margin of about 3mm of attached gingiva was needed to protect the periodontium during mastication and to dissipate fraenal pull. Properly conducted experimental work has shown that the width of attached gingiva, and even the presence or absence of an attached portion, is not of decisive importance for the maintenance of gingival health [1]. Healthy mucosa with no attached gingiva can stay healthy if it is kept clean.

## Mucogingival surgery now needs a real indication, not a measurement

The indications have been narrowed. Surgery is justified where the gingival morphology actually obstructs plaque control, where recession causes sensitivity or aesthetic issues, or, more loosely, where a thin gingival biotype overlies a tooth being moved orthodontically [2]. Thin attached gingiva on its own is not an indication.

## Recession is usually plaque or brushing trauma, not anatomy

The two commonest causes of gingival recession are plaque-induced inflammation and toothbrush trauma exposing dehiscences in alveolar bone [3]. Anatomical features, occlusal trauma, fraenal attachments, and restoration impingement are secondary [3]. So the first response to recession is OHI and brushing technique, not a graft.

citations.quote: Initially, it was felt that a margin of attached gingiva of around 3mm was required to protect the periodontium during mastication and to dissipate the pull to the gingival margin from fraenal attachments. In fact, data from properly conducted experimental work have demonstrated that the width of attached gingiva and the presence or absence of an attached portion is not of decisive importance for the maintenance of gingival health.

Where a change in the morphology of the gingival margin would improve plaque control, e.g. the presence of high fraenal attachments or deep areas of recession. Areas where recession creates root sensitivity or aesthetic problems. A very thin layer of attached gingiva overlying a tooth which is to be moved orthodontically: the evidence for this is somewhat anecdotal.

The two commonest causes are plaque-induced gingival inflammation and toothbrush trauma, revealing dehiscences in alveolar bone. Therefore, basic periodontal care and correction of faulty toothbrushing technique are the first lines of Rx. While anatomical features may contribute, these and trauma from occlusion, high fraenal attachments, and impingement from restorations are 2° considerations.

coreTruths.title: In a combined periodontal-endodontic lesion, the more pulpal it is, the better the prognosis
coreTruths.broaderContext: Combined lesions look the same on a radiograph but the order they happened in changes everything. The dental pulp can be saved; the periodontal attachment, once lost, often cannot.
coreTruths.body:
## Two diseases that look identical can mean very different futures

A combined periodontal-endodontic lesion is one where the two coalesce, regardless of which started it [1]. Both can produce a tooth with deep pocketing, periapical radiolucency, and a sinus, so the radiograph alone often does not separate them. Sensibility testing any heavily restored tooth with periodontal involvement is essential [2].

## Pulpal cause first means a treatable lesion

The greater the pulpal component, the better the prognosis [3]. A primarily endodontic lesion can be drained, root-treated, and the apparent periodontal lesion will often resolve substantially over a period of months. The advice is to defer surgery and let the endodontics work [4].

## Pure perio pathology travelling apically has the worst outlook

The worst prognosis applies to teeth where the periapical or pulpal pathology has been due entirely to apical extension of the periodontal pocket [4]. These are often diagnosed after the fact, when endodontics fails to resolve the lesion [4]. Pulp necrosis is reversible by RCT, attachment loss is largely not.

## Treat the acute first, then root-treat, then reassess for surgery

The sequence is to resolve the acute infection by drainage, with antibiotics if needed, then orthograde root canal treatment [3]. Combined apical and periodontal surgery is feasible but carries a poorer long-term prognosis [4], and the decision is best made once the endodontic component has had time to settle.

citations.quote: A combined periodontal–endodontic lesion is where both lesions coalesce regardless of whether the origin is primarily periodontal (necrotic pulp due to periodontal involvement) or primarily endodontic (periodontal tissues involved after pulp necrosis).
It is essential to sensibility test any heavily restored tooth with periodontal involvement.
First, resolve the acute infection and inflammation by drainage (&/or antibiotics), then treat with orthograde RCT (the greater the pulpal component, the better the prognosis).

The apparent periodontal lesion will often be seen to resolve to a substantial degree over a period of months, therefore, the decision to carry out surgery should be deferred. Combined apical surgery and periodontal surgery is quite feasible but carries a poorer long-term prognosis. The worst prognosis applies to those teeth where the periapical/pulpal pathology has been due entirely to apical extension of the periodontal pocket. These are often diagnosed after the fact, when endodontics completely fails to resolve the lesion.
